notes.title: Start here: Astra lessons inside the eShop sample
notes.body:
This repository is a copy of eShop, the .NET reference shop built with Blazor, ASP.NET Core, Aspire, PostgreSQL, Redis and RabbitMQ, with a bootcamp called Astra added under `eShop/astra/`. This quest uses four Astra lessons:

1. `01-lessons/05-basket-and-state.md`: the basket from the Blazor page to Redis.
2. `01-lessons/06-data-and-domain.md`: catalog stock, the Order aggregate and transactions.
3. `01-lessons/08-identity-and-security.md`: who is calling and which orders they may see.
4. `01-lessons/09-events-and-consistency.md`: what happens after the HTTP response.

Each lesson links the source files it talks about; open every link. The services you will visit are `src/WebApp`, `src/Basket.API`, `src/Catalog.API`, `src/Ordering.API`, `src/Ordering.Domain`, `src/Ordering.Infrastructure` and `src/EventBusRabbitMQ`.

The lessons are careful to say when they describe current code and when they propose a change for an exercise. The quiz is about current code, so check each statement against the linked file.

notes.title: Concept: domain methods and cached state
notes.body:
Two kinds of state show up in lessons 05 and 06.

**Domain methods.** `CatalogItem` and `Order` change their own fields through methods, and each method decides what counts as invalid. Methods differ in how they treat bad input or a wrong starting state. Read each method in full and, for every input, write down three things: does it throw, what does it change, and what does it return.

- In `CatalogItem`, compare the guards at the top of `RemoveStock` and `AddStock`.
- In `Order`, list every `Set...Status` method and the states it accepts. Note which ones call `StatusChangeException` and which simply skip.
- In `Order.AddOrderItem`, follow the branch for a product that is already on the order.

**A cached task.** `BasketState` stores a `Task` of basket items and reuses it. Find every place that sets that field back to null, and think about what a read returns in between.

Also read how `BasketState.SetQuantityAsync` treats the quantities it is given before it calls the service.

notes.title: Concept: identity, transactions and delivery
notes.body:
Lessons 08 and 09 are about boundaries that are easy to blur.

**Authentication and authorization.** Authentication says who is calling; authorization says what that caller may touch. For each Ordering query, note which predicate it filters by.

**One transaction is one database.** A local transaction can make a row and an event-log entry commit together, but it cannot include RabbitMQ or another service. Read `TransactionBehavior`, then `OrderingContext.SaveEntitiesAsync`, and write down the order of: dispatching domain events, saving, committing, publishing.

**Delivery and idempotency.** A broker redelivers only what a consumer has not acknowledged. Read the receive method of `RabbitMQEventBus` and find where the acknowledgement happens relative to the `try`/`catch`. Then read `IdentifiedCommandHandler` and `RequestManager`: when is the request marker saved, what does the `catch` return, and what does a later request with the same id see?

excerpts.quote: Learning goal: distinguish local transactions, publish intent, message delivery, and business completion.

notes.title: Why RemoveStock(5) on 3 units returns 3
notes.body:
`RemoveStock` throws only in two cases: the stock is already 0, or the requested quantity is not positive. Neither applies here. It then computes `Math.Min(quantityDesired, this.AvailableStock)`, which is 3, subtracts that, and returns it. The caller learns how much was really removed from the return value.

- Asking for more than is in stock is not an error in this method.
- Stock cannot go negative; the subtraction uses the clamped amount.
- It does not refuse partial removal; it removes what exists.

excerpts.quote: With available 3 and request 5, the result is 3 and remaining stock is 0.

notes.title: What AddStock does with a negative quantity
notes.body:
`AddStock` has no guard at the top. It checks only whether the new total would exceed `MaxStockThreshold`; 10 + (-5) = 5 does not, so the else branch runs `AvailableStock += quantity`, leaving 5. It then sets `OnReorder = false` and returns `AvailableStock - original`, which is -5. The lesson flags the missing guard as a story to fix.

- No exception is thrown for negative input in the current code.
- The call is not ignored; stock really changes.
- The sign is not flipped; the value is added as given.

excerpts.quote: It currently lacks an explicit negative-quantity guard.

notes.title: How AddStock caps at the threshold
notes.body:
90 + 25 = 115 is above the threshold of 100, so `AddStock` adds only `MaxStockThreshold - AvailableStock`, which is 10, bringing stock to 100. Either way it sets `OnReorder = false`, and it returns the real increment, `AvailableStock - original` = 10.

- Stock never exceeds the threshold, and no overstock is tracked.
- The method does not throw when the request is too large; it caps.
- The add is not rejected as a whole; the part that fits is applied.

notes.title: Why an anonymous GetBasket returns an empty basket
notes.body:
`GetBasket` carries `[AllowAnonymous]`. It reads the user id from the call context and, when there is none, returns a new empty `CustomerBasketResponse`. No error status is raised. `UpdateBasket` and `DeleteBasket` behave differently: with no identity they throw `RpcException` with `StatusCode.Unauthenticated`.

- Unauthenticated is what the write methods throw, not GetBasket.
- The basket key always comes from the identity; the request carries no buyer id.
- NotFound is used only when an update returns no basket.

excerpts.quote: var userId = context.GetUserIdentity(); if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(userId)) { return new(); }
GetBasket permits an anonymous call and returns an empty response when no user is present.

notes.title: Why a quantity of 0 never reaches the server
notes.body:
`SetQuantityAsync` finds the row for the product. For a positive quantity it updates the row; otherwise it removes the row from the list. It then clears the cache and sends the remaining rows with `UpdateBasketAsync`. So setting 0 in the UI means remove this product, and the request simply lacks the row.

- No zero-quantity row is sent; the row is removed first.
- 0 is not rejected; it has a meaning in this method.
- The whole basket is not deleted; only that row goes.

excerpts.quote: Zero quantity in the UI has another meaning: BasketState removes the row before sending the replacement list.

notes.title: Why a deleted basket can still show items
notes.body:
`FetchBasketItemsAsync` returns `_cachedBasket ??= FetchCoreAsync()`, so once a task is cached it is reused. `AddAsync` and `SetQuantityAsync` set `_cachedBasket = null` before updating. `DeleteBasketAsync` only calls the service: it does not clear the cache and does not notify subscribers. A later read on the same `BasketState` gets the old completed task, with the old items.

- Nothing resets the cache on delete.
- The cached task is not cancelled; it already completed.
- Reads do not refetch while a cached task exists.

notes.title: When Ordering dispatches domain events
notes.body:
`SaveEntitiesAsync` first awaits `_mediator.DispatchDomainEventsAsync(this)` and only then `base.SaveChangesAsync`. Domain event handlers use the same scoped `OrderingContext`, so whatever they change is saved in that one call, inside whatever transaction `TransactionBehavior` opened. The long comment in the method describes both options; the code takes the before option.

- Handlers do not run after the save, so they do not get separate transactions.
- Nothing runs in parallel; each step is awaited.
- Domain events are in-process MediatR notifications, not integration-log entries.

notes.title: Why a failed handler still acknowledges the message
notes.body:
The receive method wraps processing in `try`/`catch`. The `catch` logs a warning and tags the activity, and does not rethrow. `BasicAckAsync` comes after the whole block, so it runs on success and on failure alike. The broker deletes an acknowledged message, so a failed handler loses its delivery. The comment says a production app should use a dead-letter exchange.

- No reject or requeue call exists in this path.
- No dead-letter exchange is configured; the comment names it as missing work.
- The message is acknowledged right away, not held until a restart.

excerpts.quote: // Even on exception we take the message off the queue.

notes.title: Why a retry after a failure reports success
notes.body:
`IdentifiedCommandHandler` saves the request marker with `CreateRequestForCommandAsync` before it sends the inner command. If the inner command throws, the `catch` returns `default`, which is false for a bool, and swallows the exception. With no exception escaping, the outer `TransactionBehavior` commits, so the marker is stored. The retry finds the marker and returns `CreateResultForDuplicateRequest()`, which is `true` for create-order. The client sees success, yet no order exists.

- The command is not run again; the marker says it was seen.
- The duplicate path returns a value; it does not throw.
- The retry does not repeat false; it takes the duplicate branch.

excerpts.quote: return true; // Ignore duplicate requests for creating order.

notes.title: Why SetPaidStatus is silent in the wrong state
notes.body:
`SetPaidStatus` wraps its whole body in `if (OrderStatus == OrderStatus.StockConfirmed)`. In AwaitingValidation the condition is false, so the method adds no event, changes nothing and returns normally. Other transitions are stricter: `SetShippedStatus` calls `StatusChangeException` and throws when the order is not Paid. The lesson's state-machine lab asks you to record exactly these differences.

- No exception: this method has no else branch.
- It does not jump to Paid; the guard blocks it.
- It does not move to StockConfirmed; that is a different method.

excerpts.quote: For each transition method, record valid starting states and whether an invalid call throws or leaves the state unchanged.

notes.title: How AddOrderItem merges a repeated product
notes.body:
`AddOrderItem` first looks for an existing line with the same product id. When it finds one, it replaces the discount only if the new one is higher, then calls `AddUnits`. The first call created a line with 1 unit and discount 2; the second call raises the discount to 5 and adds 2 units, giving one line with 3 units and discount 5. The unit price of the second call is not used.

- No second line is created for the same product.
- The lower discount does not stay; the higher one wins.
- Units are added, not replaced.

notes.title: Why Bob can read Alice's order
notes.body:
The orders route group requires an authenticated caller, and Bob is one. `GetOrderAsync` in `OrdersApi` passes the id straight to `OrderQueries.GetOrderAsync`, which loads with `FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id)` and no buyer predicate. The order exists, so the API returns 200 with Alice's data. The list endpoint is different: it filters by `o.Buyer.IdentityGuid == userId`. Lesson 08 turns this gap into an exercise.

- No buyer filter exists on the detail query, so there is no 404 for Bob.
- Nothing checks ownership, so there is no 403.
- Bob's token is valid; authentication passes.
